Le 24 avril dernier, alors qu’il est che: On April 24, while at home with his girlfriend, Lloys Chatel-Elie, 25, got a visit from the SPVM, who had been called about an illegal gathering. Lloys opened the door while filming the encounter on his phone. “They told me they'd received a complaint about a party,” he says. Lloys decided to cooperate with the three officers and invited them into his home. “I told them there was no party, it was just me and my girlfriend, and I invited them in to check,” he explains.
Mais la situation dégénère rapidement. D: But the situation quickly went downhill. In an excerpt of the video, the officers can be heard asking Lloys to show them his ID. He then suggests the officers step out of his home so he can hand over his ID outside.
Les policiers présents, qui auraient ref: The officers, who reportedly refused to identify themselves, then carried out a rough arrest. Lloys was injured in the head during the intervention. The young man remains shaken by the incident. Since then, he avoids any contact with peace officers. “I just don't want anything to do with them,” he says. The SPVM's media relations team declined to comment on the matter.
Depuis le début de la pandémie, plusieur: Since the start of the pandemic, there have been several altercations with law enforcement. How do you handle a situation like that? Lloys Chatel-Elie gives us his take on how to react if you're arrested in order to reduce the risk of police brutality.
Y faisant écho, Fo Niemi, co-fondateur e: Echoing him, Fo Niemi, co-founder and executive director of the Centre de recherche-action sur les relations raciales (CRARR), offers advice on how to behave during a police intervention to avoid danger as much as possible.
Il est possible qu’il n’y ait aucun témo: There may be no witnesses on the scene when police step in. “If you're alone, call someone close to you on your cellphone and leave the line open for the whole intervention so that the person can hear the conversation,” Niemi recommends. “When you're alone, you're completely at the mercy of the police. It's then harder to prove your version of events if there are no witnesses,” he adds.
Si la police vous demande une pièce d’id: If police ask you for ID, or for your vehicle papers if you're on the road, Niemi suggests handing them over right away. “Under the Highway Safety Code and under the Criminal Code of Canada, if you refuse to show your papers, you risk being charged with obstructing police work.
C’est une accusation criminelle, rappell: That's a criminal charge,” he points out. “If you don't respond to the officers' requests, or if you speak in an aggressive tone, you risk bruising their ego and getting into trouble.” Niemi adds that in a traffic stop, only the driver of the vehicle is required to identify themselves and provide their papers. “Passengers aren't required to show ID, unless it's to write up a statement of offence.
Par exemple, si vous êtes passager et qu: “For example, if you're a passenger and you're not wearing your seat belt, you can be fined. However, some officers ask everyone for ID in order to gather information about the people in the vehicle, especially when they're young Black men. That's illegal,” he stresses.
Lorsqu’on a affaire à la police, M. Niem: When dealing with police, Niemi recommends avoiding arguing with them. “People have the right to ask questions, of course, but if the officer isn't friendly and doesn't answer, don't challenge their authority,” he says. “If you resist repeatedly, the officer can arrest you for obstruction.”
Une entrave est un refus d’obtempérer à: Obstruction is a refusal to comply with an officer's request. “Even if you know something is illegal or that the law doesn't require it, don't argue with the police. Hand over your ID and file a complaint afterward,” he advises.
Selon Lloys Chatel-Elie, pour éviter tou: According to Lloys Chatel-Elie, the best way to avoid danger is to go along with the officers' requests. “You never know with the police, but I think if you do what they ask, in the end they'll have no reason to hurt you.” He also suggests asking the officers for permission before making any move. “If you have to do something, ask them,” he advises.
Lorsque les policiers se sont présentés: When the officers showed up at his home, Lloys started recording the intervention even before opening the door. “It was a good thing I took out my phone beforehand, because they could have thought I had a weapon,” he says. Having a video of an intervention can be crucial. Niemi notes, however, that it's important to take certain precautions.
« ll ne faut pas filmer de manière à emp: “You must not film in a way that prevents, compromises or hinders the work of police officers,” he explains, adding that it's best not to get close to the officers. This advice also applies if you witness an arrest and want to film it.
Les policiers demandent habituellement à: Police usually ask that the hands of the people they're dealing with be visible at all times. “They don't know what you have on you,” Niemi illustrates, specifying that you absolutely must keep your hands out of your pockets. “And if you're pulled over on the road, don't get out of your vehicle,” he adds.
Lloys conseille par ailleurs d’éviter de: Lloys also advises avoiding sudden movements. “It gives them a reason to react,” he says. “Their excuse is that they feel threatened.” Officers may indeed judge that they are in danger and react.
« Si vous êtes en état d’arrestation, n’: “If you're under arrest, don't resist. People, especially men, tend to defend themselves when they're being handcuffed. We advise against it because it risks making the intervention more violent. The officer can also charge you with resisting arrest, which is another criminal offence.
Et si jamais vous frappez ou touchez un: “And if you ever hit or touch an officer, you could face a third criminal charge, assaulting a police officer,” Niemi sums up. He also explains that when several charges of this kind pile up, the financial consequences can be enormous, as proceedings stretch over months, even years in some cases.
« Vous serez épuisé sur le plan financie: “You'll be financially drained if you have to pay for a defence lawyer over such a long period,” he warns. It's important to say here that this advice has no legal value: these are simply strategies that an individual who wants to reduce the risk of becoming a victim of police brutality during a stop can adopt.
Malheureusement, trop souvent pour les p: Unfortunately, all too often for racialized people, being in the right does not prevent racial profiling and police violence, just as following this advice does not guarantee fair treatment by police.
Me Denis Barrette, avocat criminaliste,: Criminal lawyer Denis Barrette explains that citizens have rights and that police officers have obligations. “A police officer is not an ordinary citizen, and we tell ordinary citizens: ignorance of the law is no excuse. A police officer must also know their obligations. We have to make sure they know them and that they apply them,” he says.
Un policier est un agent de l’État qui d: “A police officer is an agent of the state with an enormous amount of power. Given the powers they hold, they must be trained and well informed about their obligations, and their training must be up to date.”
L’avocat cite alors<l1> la Charte des dr: The lawyer then cites<l1> the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms</l1>, which prohibits racial, social, economic, political and other forms of profiling. “In the exercise of their duties, police officers absolutely must act in accordance with the rules on this.” In concrete terms, there are several things to keep in mind during a police intervention. “It's always better to make sure everything goes smoothly; don't forget that the officer has a firearm, as well as material and physical force,” Barrette reminds us. “But if you've been subjected to an unlawful arrest or detention, there are remedies.”
Quoi qu’il arrive, il est important de s: Whatever happens, it's important to know that an individual can invoke their rights. In the case of detention, a police officer has obligations toward the person they are detaining. “They must give the right to a lawyer and the right to remain silent in clear language,” Barrette explains. An individual also does not have to answer police questions, unless those questions are meant to identify them. Police are also obliged to allow a person they are detaining to call a lawyer, who will be able to give them legal advice and guide them.
Si un individu n’a pas d’avocat, les pol: If an individual doesn't have a lawyer, police will turn to legal aid, the Barreau's on-call service or another free legal resource, which they will put in contact with the detained person. The conversation between the lawyer and the detainee is confidential.
Plusieurs facteurs, touchant notamment l: Several factors, including the type of offence and the length of the detention, must however be met for an arrested person to be able to call a lawyer.
Au cours d’une intervention, les agents: During an intervention, police officers are required to identify themselves. You can therefore ask them for their names and badge numbers. This information also appears on the badge they are required to wear.
Dans le cas d’une intervention policière: If a police intervention goes wrong, Barrette strongly advises gathering evidence as quickly as possible. You can write an account of the events, note every detail of the harm suffered and take photos (of damage, for example), obtain footage captured on a cellphone or surveillance camera, get medical certificates if you were injured and contact witnesses.
Ces documents peuvent ensuite être remis: These documents can then be given to a lawyer, presented to a legal aid organization and filed with a police ethics complaint. Barrette stresses the importance of acting as quickly as possible. “When someone is the victim of abuse, their first reaction is to withdraw, to try to forget the bad memory, and often the evidence fades.”
« On ne peut pas interpeller quelqu’un p: “You can't stop someone for no reason. If you're walking down the street, a police officer must tell you why they're stopping you,” Barrette insists. An intervention cannot take place without reasonable grounds, even in cases where rights are reduced, for example when you're driving a car, you have to know why you're being stopped. “The officer is obliged to give the reason for their intervention. It's an obligation, even if you don't ask,” the lawyer says.
